a: Elijah
p: Elijah's name is itself his message: Eli-yahu, "my God is Yah," that is, the LORD.
b: Elijah walks into the story with no family line and no call scene, only a name and a hometown. The name Eliyyahu means "my God is Yahu," a short form of the divine name YHWH, which this translation writes as "the LORD" in capitals. In a kingdom where Ahab has built a temple to Baal in Samaria (16:32), the name is a creed. The people's cry at the end of the contest, "The LORD, he is the God!" (18:39), says the same thing his name says. The sudden entrance has led readers to compare him with Melchizedek (Genesis 14:18), another figure with no stated parents, and Jewish tradition made much of the fact that his death is never told (2 Kings 2:11).

a: whom I stand before
p: To "stand before" a king is to be in his service, ready for orders. Elijah serves a greater king than Ahab.
b: In Hebrew a servant "stands before" his master: the phrase describes courtiers waiting on a king (10:8; 12:8) and priests and Levites serving the LORD (Deuteronomy 10:8). Many translations simply say "whom I serve." This translation keeps the picture, because the scene depends on it: Elijah stands in front of Ahab, but he says he really stands before someone else. He uses the same oath again before Obadiah (18:15), and Elisha takes it over (2 Kings 3:14; 2 Kings 5:16).
orig: אֲשֶׁר עָמַדְתִּי לְפָנָיו ('asher 'amadti lefanav), "before whom I stand"

a: these coming years
p: A Phoenician history quoted by Josephus mentions a long drought in the reign of Jezebel's father.
b: Josephus quotes Menander of Ephesus (on whom see the note on 16:31) as saying that in the reign of Ithobaal, Jezebel's father, there was a lack of rain that lasted a year, until Ithobaal prayed and thunder came (Josephus, Antiquities 8.13.2). Josephus himself linked this with Elijah's drought. The note is late and second-hand, and one year is not three, so it proves little. But it shows that droughts in Phoenicia in this period were remembered, and that the people of Tyre credited their own king's prayers for ending one.

a: no dew and no rain
p: Baal was the god of storm and rain. A drought announced in the LORD's name strikes at the heart of his worship.
b: In the myths found at Ugarit in Syria (about 1300 BC), Baal, the storm god, rides the clouds and sends the rains; when he is swallowed by Death, the land dries up. In the Aqhat story a father curses the land: "Seven years may Baal fail, eight the Rider of the Clouds: no dew, no rain." The words of 17:1 sound like a deliberate answer: the LORD, not Baal, holds back dew and rain. Verdict: a real and intended contrast. Israel did not borrow its God from these myths, but the Elijah stories are told against them, and the drought sets up the question Carmel will settle (18:24).

a: unless I give the word
t: The prayer that shut the sky
p: Deuteronomy warned that worship of other gods would shut the sky. Luke, James and Revelation all remember this drought.
b: Elijah's word carries out the covenant warning: "He will shut up the sky, and there will be no rain" (Deuteronomy 11:17; see also Deuteronomy 28:23–24). The New Testament takes up the scene three times. Jesus reminds his hometown that the sky was shut for three and a half years and Elijah was sent to a foreign widow (Luke 4:25–26). James holds up Elijah as "a man just like us" whose prayer stopped the rain and later brought it back (James 5:17–18), although 1 Kings itself does not say Elijah prayed for the drought. Revelation's two witnesses "have authority to shut the sky" (Revelation 11:6).

a: the ravens
p: The Hebrew 'orvim means ravens. A few readers have taken the same letters as "Arabs" or as townspeople.
b: 'Orvim is the ordinary word for ravens, birds the Law calls unclean (Leviticus 11:15). That is part of the wonder: God feeds his prophet by birds no Israelite would eat. Because the same consonants can be read 'arvim, "Arabs," or taken as people from a place named Orev, some interpreters (already known to medieval Jewish commentators, and some modern ones) have pictured human helpers. Nothing in the text points that way, and every ancient version has birds. The Talmud asks where the ravens found bread and meat and answers, with a smile, from King Ahab's own kitchen (Bavli Hullin 5a).

a: Zarephath, a town of Sidon
p: God sends Elijah into Phoenicia, the land of Jezebel's father and of Baal, to be fed by a foreign widow.
b: Zarephath (Greek Sarepta, today Sarafand in Lebanon) lay on the coast between Tyre and Sidon. James Pritchard excavated it between 1969 and 1974 and found a Phoenician town with pottery workshops and a small shrine; an inscription there names the goddess Tanit-Astarte. Sending Elijah here is a bold move: the LORD feeds his prophet in the heartland of Baal and of Ethbaal, "king of the Sidonians" and Jezebel's father (16:31). Jesus used the story to shock his hometown: there were many widows in Israel, but Elijah was sent only to one in Sidon (Luke 4:25–26).

a: By the life of the LORD your God
t: A foreigner swears by the LORD
p: The widow knows the LORD's name but calls him "your God." By the end of the chapter she confesses his word is true.
b: The widow takes an oath by Israel's God, perhaps because she recognizes Elijah as an Israelite holy man. "Your God" keeps a distance: he is the stranger's God, not hers. Jewish and Christian readers have traced her journey across the chapter, from "your God" (17:12) to "the LORD's word in your mouth is true" (17:24). Rabbinic tradition went further and made her son the prophet Jonah, another Israelite later sent to foreigners (Jerusalem Talmud Sukkah 5:1; Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 33). Christian readers from Luke onward saw her as a first sign that God's mercy reaches beyond Israel (Luke 4:26).

a: Do not be afraid
p: Elijah asks a starving mother to feed him before her son. Readers have heard it as faith, test or harshness.
b: Taken on its own, the request sounds cruel: a stranger asks a widow to give him the last meal she has. The promise in the next verse changes it. Elijah does not ask for her food as payment; he asks her to act on the LORD's word before she sees the result, just as Elijah himself acted on the word at Kerith (17:5). Christian preachers have often linked her to the poor widow who gave "her whole living" (Mark 12:44). Others note that the story does not praise her as a hero of faith: she simply does what the prophet says, and the jar keeps giving.

a: The flour in the jar did not give out
p: The miracle has close cousins in Elisha's jar of oil and in the gospel feedings.
b: The next generation tells the same kind of story about Elisha, who fills a widow's empty jars with oil to pay her debts (2 Kings 4:1–7) and feeds a hundred men with twenty loaves (2 Kings 4:42–44). The gospels' feeding stories echo Elisha's directly, and through him Elijah's (Mark 6:35–44; John 6:9). Readers who take the stories as history see God's care for the poor in a famine; those who read them as legend see a type of tale told about holy men across the ancient world. Both readings agree on the point: the LORD, not Baal, gives grain and oil (Hosea 2:8).

a: until not a breath remained in him
p: The text says no breath was left in him. Most readers take that as death; a few see a deep coma.
b: The Hebrew does not use the word "died" here, only that no breath (neshamah) was left. The mother's words ("to put my son to death") and Elijah's prayer ("Have you... put her son to death?") both treat him as dead, and so does the end of the story. Josephus, retelling the story, says the boy appeared to be dead, and some modern readers allow that he was close to death but not dead. The text as told means a return from death, and later Jewish and Christian tradition took it that way (Hebrews 11:35).

a: what is there between you and me?
t: "What is there between you and me?"
p: An idiom of protest: "What do you want with me?" or "Why are you mixing in my life?"
b: The Hebrew is literally "What to me and to you?" It pushes someone away: what business do we have together? It appears in 2 Samuel when David rebukes the sons of Zeruiah (2 Samuel 16:10; 2 Samuel 19:22), and in the gospels in Greek, when the demons cry out to Jesus (Mark 1:24) and when Jesus answers his mother at Cana (John 2:4). Here a grieving mother uses it to say: since you came, my son has died. The holy man has brought God's attention, and so God's judgment, into her house.
orig: מַה־לִּי וָלָךְ (mah-li valakh), "what to me and to you?"

a: to bring my guilt to mind
p: The mother assumes her son died because a man of God made God notice her sin.
b: Many ancient people believed that a holy person's presence brought hidden sin to light, and that illness and death were punishment. The widow does not say what her sin was. Rabbinic and Christian readers both use the verse to show a common but mistaken link between suffering and personal guilt, the same link Job's friends make and Jesus rejects (John 9:2–3). The story does not confirm her fear: Elijah takes her complaint to God, and God answers with life, not a verdict.

a: lay stretched out full length
p: The verb means "stretched himself out," literally "measured himself," body to body over the boy.
b: The Hebrew vayyitmoded comes from madad, "to measure," and appears only here in this form. The picture is of Elijah lying full length on the boy, matching him limb for limb. Elisha does the same, mouth to mouth and hand to hand (2 Kings 4:34), and Paul throws himself on Eutychus (Acts 20:10). Some have compared it to warming or to breathing into the body; the Greek translation says Elijah "breathed" on the boy (see the variant on this verse). The text itself gives the credit to prayer: the LORD heard, and the life came back (17:22).

a: The boy's life came back inside him, and he lived.
t: The first raising of the dead
p: This is the first time in the Bible that someone who has died is brought back to life.
b: The word for life here is nefesh, the living self or breath. Its return makes this the Bible's first story of a dead person raised, followed by Elisha's raisings (2 Kings 4:32–37; 2 Kings 13:21) and those of Jesus and the apostles (Luke 7:11–17; Acts 9:36–41). Readers differ: many Jews and Christians read it as a real miracle; critical scholars often see a legend told in prophetic circles, like the Elisha stories; others stress the theological point, that the LORD, not Baal or Death, has power over life. The Talmud says three keys stay in God's own hand: rain, birth and the raising of the dead (Bavli Taanit 2a). In its telling, Elijah held the key of rain, and to receive the key of the dead for this boy he had to give the rain key back, which is why rain returns in 18:1 (Bavli Sanhedrin 113a).

a: gave him to his mother
p: Luke tells Jesus' raising of a widow's son at Nain in words that recall this verse.
b: When Jesus raises the only son of a widow at the town gate of Nain, Luke says that "Jesus gave him to his mother" (Luke 7:15), the very words of the Greek translation of 17:23. The crowd then cries that "a great prophet" has appeared (Luke 7:16). Luke seems to want readers to think of Elijah, whom he has already named in Jesus' first sermon (Luke 4:25–26). Nain, like Zarephath, is a story of a widow, a dead son, and a prophet at the town gate.

a: the LORD's word in your mouth is true
p: Chapter 17 is about the word of the LORD, and it ends with a foreign woman saying that word is true.
b: The phrase "the word of the LORD" or its like runs all through the chapter (17:2, 17:5, 17:8, 17:16). Elijah announces the drought by his "word," and each scene proves the word reliable: the ravens come, the jar does not fail, the boy lives. The last line belongs to the widow, who is not an Israelite: "the LORD's word in your mouth is true." The Hebrew emet, "truth," also means "reliable, faithful." The next chapter tests the same claim before all Israel.

a: in the third year
t: Three years, or three and a half?
p: 1 Kings says the word came "in the third year." Jesus and James speak of three years and six months.
b: The count here may run from Elijah's stay at Zarephath or from the start of the drought; either way it falls short of the "three years and six months" in Luke 4:25 and James 5:17. Some harmonize: the dry season had already begun before Elijah spoke, so the whole drought was longer than the time counted here. Others think the New Testament uses three and a half as a set number for a time of judgment, half of seven, as in Daniel 7:25 and Revelation 11:2–3, where the two witnesses also shut the sky. Both readings are old; the second explains why two separate New Testament writers give the same figure.

a: Obadiah
p: Obadiah means "servant of the LORD." The rabbis identified him with the prophet whose book bears the name.
b: Obadiah serves Ahab at the highest level and fears the LORD at the same time, hiding prophets under Jezebel's nose. Readers have long debated whether he is a model of quiet faith inside a corrupt government or a man compromised by his post; the narrator plainly admires him (18:3, 18:12). The Talmud identifies him with the prophet Obadiah and calls him an Edomite convert, fitting a prophet who preached against Edom (Bavli Sanhedrin 39b). Christian writers often compared him with Joseph in Pharaoh's court and with Daniel in Babylon.

a: the man in charge of the royal house
p: The title "over the house" belonged to the king's chief steward, one of the highest offices in the kingdom.
b: The officer "over the house" ran the royal estate and household. Solomon had one (4:6), Hezekiah's was Shebna and then Eliakim (Isaiah 22:15–22), and Joseph held the same kind of office in Egypt (Genesis 41:40). Seal impressions from Judah carry the title "who is over the house," and a tomb inscription from the village of Silwan near Jerusalem names a royal steward with the same title. Obadiah is no small servant; he is near the top of Ahab's government.

a: Jezebel was wiping out the prophets of the LORD
t: A persecution told only in passing
p: The killing of the LORD's prophets is never narrated; Obadiah, Elijah and later Jehu mention it in passing.
b: 1 Kings never narrates Jezebel's campaign against the prophets; it is mentioned in passing by Obadiah, by Elijah (19:10, 19:14) and later by Jehu (2 Kings 9:7). Historians who read the story critically ask whether a queen could have killed many prophets, and suspect the later writer has made her the face of all Baal worship. Others note that royal women in Phoenicia and elsewhere could hold great power, as Athaliah, Ahab's daughter, later did in Judah (2 Kings 11). Either way, the hiding of a hundred prophets shows that the LORD's prophets were numerous, organized and known to the court.

a: in groups of fifty in the cave
p: The Hebrew of 18:4 has a single "fifty." Many scholars think a second "fifty" dropped out, as 18:13 suggests.
b: In 18:4 the Masoretic Text reads literally "and he hid them, fifty men in the cave." In 18:13, where Obadiah tells the same story, it reads "fifty, fifty men," the Hebrew way of saying "by fifties." Many scholars think a second "fifty" fell out of 18:4 when a copyist's eye skipped from one word to the identical word next to it (haplography); the Greek reads "by fifties" here. The noun is singular with the article, "the cave," which can mean "a cave for each group" or one large cave. Some modern versions say "two caves," but that is an inference from a hundred men in groups of fifty, not a reading of any ancient copy; the Latin Vulgate has simply "in caves." Carmel and the hills of Samaria are full of limestone caves. This translation reads "in groups of fifty" in both verses and keeps the singular "cave."
orig: חֲמִשִּׁים אִישׁ בַּמְּעָרָה (chamishshim 'ish bamme'arah), "fifty men in the cave"

a: Check every spring of water and every stream bed
t: A king who looks for grass
p: While his people starve, Ahab's first worry is his horses. The narrator lets the detail speak.
b: Ahab and his steward split the land to look for grazing. Some readers see a responsible king trying to save the army's chariot horses, which the Assyrian records say he had in great numbers. Others read the scene as quiet satire: the king searches springs and stream beds for grass, when the reason for the drought, according to Elijah, is in his own palace (18:18). The horses also recall Deuteronomy's warning that a king must not gather many horses (Deuteronomy 17:16).

a: the LORD's Spirit will carry you off
p: Obadiah fears Elijah will vanish, as prophets were believed to do, carried away by the Spirit.
b: Elijah seems to have had a reputation for appearing and disappearing. After he is taken up, the sons of the prophets search for him in case "the Spirit of the LORD" has dropped him on some mountain (2 Kings 2:16). Ezekiel is lifted and carried by the Spirit (Ezekiel 3:12–14; Ezekiel 8:3), and Philip is snatched away after baptizing the Ethiopian (Acts 8:39). Obadiah's fear is very practical: if Elijah disappears, the king will kill the messenger.

a: the LORD of Armies
p: First use in 1 Kings of YHWH tseva'ot, "the LORD of hosts" in older Bibles.
b: Tseva'ot is the plural of tsava', "army, host." This translation renders the title "the LORD of Armies" in every book, as the WEB and CSB also do. The armies may be Israel's troops, the stars or the angels of God's court; in Kings the last is close at hand, since Micaiah will see "all the army of heaven" standing beside the LORD's throne (22:19). Elijah uses the title in his oath (18:15) and in his complaint at Horeb, "the LORD, the God of Armies" (19:10, 19:14). Older English Bibles say "the LORD of hosts"; some modern ones say "the LORD Almighty," following the Greek pantokratōr.

a: the one who brings trouble on Israel
p: The verb 'akhar ties Elijah, in Ahab's eyes, to Achan, whose sin brought disaster on all Israel.
b: 'Akhar means to stir up, to bring ruin on a group. Joshua uses it of Achan: "Why have you brought trouble on us? The LORD will bring trouble on you this day" (Joshua 7:25), and Jonathan uses it of his father Saul (1 Samuel 14:29). Ahab blames the drought on the man who announced it. Elijah turns the charge around: the trouble came from the king who abandoned the LORD's commands (18:18). The question of the chapter, who is really to blame for the drought, will be settled by fire.

a: you went after the Baals
p: The Baal of Jezebel's court was probably a god of Tyre, either Baal Shamem, "lord of heaven," or Melqart.
b: "Baal" means "lord" and was the title of many local gods; the plural "the Baals" covers them all. Ahab built a temple of Baal in Samaria for Jezebel (16:32). Since she was a princess of Tyre and Sidon, scholars have proposed Melqart, the city god of Tyre, or Baal Shamem, "lord of the heavens," a sky and storm god widely worshiped in Phoenicia. The storm god fits the story best: the contest is over rain and fire from the sky. On Jezebel's father Ethbaal and the Phoenician sources, see the note on 16:31.

a: Mount Carmel
p: Carmel, "garden land," is the green ridge that runs to the sea at modern Haifa, on the border with Phoenicia.
b: The Carmel ridge rises to about 1,800 feet (550 m) above the sea and catches the winter rains, so it stays green longer than most of the land (Amos 1:2; Isaiah 35:2). It stood on the border between Israel and Tyre, a fitting place to settle whose god ruled the region. The Roman historian Tacitus says that in his day Carmel was the name of both a mountain and a god, with an altar but no image or temple (Tacitus, Histories 2.78). Christian tradition places the contest at el-Muhraqa, "the place of burning," a Carmelite site at the southeast end of the ridge, above the Kishon River.

a: the four hundred prophets of Asherah who are fed at Jezebel's table
p: The prophets of Asherah are summoned but never appear in the Hebrew story again. The Greek adds them at 18:22.
b: Only the 450 prophets of Baal take part in the contest (18:22, 18:25) and only they are killed (18:40). In the Hebrew the 400 prophets of Asherah vanish. The Greek names them again at 18:22, so that they are present at the contest (see the variant there); most scholars take that as a scribe's harmonizing addition. Some readers think they stayed away, under Jezebel's protection; many critical scholars think a later scribe added them, since Asherah worship was a constant target of the Deuteronomistic writers. To "eat at the table" of the king or queen means to be fed and paid by the court, like Mephibosheth at David's table (2 Samuel 9:7). Jezebel's prophets are, in effect, state employees.

a: limp along on two crutches
p: The Hebrew image is of limping or hopping on two crutches or branches. Many Bibles say "two opinions."
b: Elijah's question uses pasach, "to limp, to hop," and se'ippim, a rare word related to "branches" (Isaiah 17:6) and to "divided thoughts" (Psalm 119:113). The KJV has "halt between two opinions"; others say "waver" or "hobble on two crutches." The picture is of someone trying to walk two ways at once, or leaning on two supports that will not hold. It also sets up a bitter pun: the prophets of Baal will "limp" around their altar (18:26), using the same verb. Israel, Elijah implies, is dancing Baal's dance.

a: I alone am left as a prophet of the LORD
p: Elijah says he is the only prophet left, though Obadiah has just told him of a hundred in hiding.
b: The claim is strong on purpose: in the contest it is one against 450. But readers notice that it is not quite true, since a hundred of the LORD's prophets are hiding in a cave (18:13). Some take it to mean that Elijah alone is still prophesying in public. Others see the first sign of a weakness that comes out at Horeb, where he says it twice more (19:10, 19:14) and God answers that seven thousand have not bowed to Baal (19:18). Paul quotes the Horeb version to make a point about the faithful few (Romans 11:2–4).

a: Whichever god answers with fire
t: Fire on the storm god's ground
p: Baal was the god of lightning. Elijah lets the contest be fought on the very ground Baal was said to rule.
b: In Canaanite texts and pictures Baal holds a club and a spear of lightning, and the Ugaritic poems speak of him "giving his voice" in thunder and flashing his lightning to the earth. A test of fire from the sky is a test Baal's followers should win. That is why the people agree at once that it is fair. Verdict: the link is real and deliberate. The story claims that the LORD does what Baal was believed to do: sends the fire, and then the rain (18:38, 18:45).

a: the altar that had been made
p: The Hebrew says "the altar that he had made"; the Greek says "that they had made."
b: The Hebrew verb is singular, 'asah, "he made." It may be impersonal, "that someone had made," or a copying slip for the plural 'asu, which the Greek reads. A few take "he" as Ahab, who had built Baal's altar in Samaria (16:32), but this altar stands on Carmel. The Plain English uses a passive so as not to name a maker the text leaves unclear.

a: he has stepped away
p: Elijah's mockery includes a word, sig, that many take as a polite way of saying Baal is in the toilet.
b: Elijah taunts with three guesses. Siach may mean "musing" or "busy"; sig, from a root meaning "to move away," is often taken, by ancient readers and by modern scholars such as Gary Rendsburg, as a way of saying "he has gone off to relieve himself"; the third is "he is on a journey." Translations divide: some keep a vague "busy," others print the crude sense. This translation keeps the vague English, which hides a joke the first hearers probably caught. The point either way is mockery: a god who has to be woken up, or who has stepped out, is no god.

a: Or maybe he's asleep, and he'll wake up.
p: Elijah's "maybe he's asleep" may poke fun at the belief that Baal died and rose with the seasons.
b: In the Ugaritic Baal cycle, Baal goes down into the throat of Mot, Death, and the land withers; later he returns and the rain comes back. Older scholars spoke of a "dying and rising god"; many now think that label too broad, but Baal's absence and return are clearly in the texts. Elijah's jibe would then cut close: the god who goes away and must be roused. Israel's psalms answer that the LORD "will not slumber" (Psalm 121:4), though they can also beg him to "wake up" (Psalm 44:23). Verdict: a likely echo, though the mockery works without it.

a: they cut themselves, as was their custom
p: Cutting the body was a known rite in Canaan; Israel's law forbade it.
b: In the Ugaritic poems the god El, mourning Baal, gashes his cheeks, chin and arms. Jeremiah describes worshipers who cut themselves (Jeremiah 16:6; Jeremiah 41:5), and Hosea speaks of people who gash themselves for grain and wine (Hosea 7:14, in the Greek and many translations). The Law says: "Do not slash your bodies for someone who has died" (Leviticus 19:28; see Deuteronomy 14:1). "As was their custom" shows the narrator knew this as a regular rite, not a moment of panic: blood offered to move a god to act.

a: they kept on prophesying
p: The verb here describes ecstatic behavior: shouting, dancing and trance, not foretelling.
b: Hitnabbe', the reflexive form of "prophesy," often means behaving like a prophet in trance: Saul strips off his clothes and lies on the ground when he "prophesies" (1 Samuel 19:23–24), and bands of prophets prophesy to music (1 Samuel 10:5). Ecstatic prophets were known across the region; an Egyptian report from Byblos, the story of Wenamun (about 1075 BC), describes a young man seized in a frenzy who delivers a message from the god. Many translations add "frantic" or "raved." The Plain English keeps the verb and lets the context show what kind of prophesying this was.

a: until the time when the grain offering goes up
p: Elijah waits for the afternoon offering. Jewish afternoon prayer, called Minchah, is tied to this hour.
b: The minchah, "grain offering," was presented each afternoon with the evening lamb (Exodus 29:38–41; Numbers 28:4–8). Elijah prays at that hour (18:36), the time when Ezra and Daniel also pray (Ezra 9:5; Daniel 9:21). Jewish afternoon prayer is still called Minchah, and the Talmud tells worshipers to be careful about it, "for Elijah was answered only at the Minchah prayer" (Bavli Berakhot 6b). That Elijah keeps the Jerusalem hour of offering on a northern mountain is part of his message that the LORD is God of all Israel.

a: he mended the LORD's altar, which had been knocked down
p: Deuteronomy allows sacrifice only at the place the LORD chooses. Why does Elijah rebuild an altar on Carmel?
b: The writer of Kings judges every king by whether he worshiped at the one chosen place, Jerusalem (Deuteronomy 12:5–14), and condemns the "high places." Yet here the prophet repairs an old altar of the LORD on Carmel and the LORD accepts the offering. The rabbis answered that a true prophet may set aside a law for a moment in an emergency, and they cite this scene (Bavli Yevamot 90b). Critical scholars suggest the story is older than the Deuteronomistic rule and kept its northern setting. Others note that for the northern tribes, cut off from Jerusalem since Jeroboam (12:26–33), no other lawful altar was available.

a: twelve stones
p: In the northern kingdom of ten tribes, Elijah builds with twelve stones: one Israel, as at Sinai and the Jordan.
b: The twelve stones recall the twelve standing stones Moses set up at Sinai (Exodus 24:4) and the twelve stones from the Jordan (Joshua 4:3–9). By naming Jacob, the one the LORD renamed Israel (Genesis 35:10), Elijah reminds the northern kingdom that it is not the whole of Israel and that its true identity comes from the LORD, not from Ahab or from the split under Jeroboam (12:16–20). Early Christian readers also linked the twelve stones with the twelve apostles.

a: the size of a plot sown with two seahs of seed
p: The Hebrew can mean a ditch around an area sown with two seahs of seed, or a ditch that would hold that much seed.
b: Beit sa'tayim zera' is literally "a house of two seahs of seed." Fields were measured by the seed needed to sow them (Leviticus 27:16), so many scholars read an area: the ditch ran around a plot that size, a sizable space. Others take "house" as a container, so that the ditch could hold about two seahs, roughly 4 to 7 gallons; the KJV and most modern versions read it that way. This translation takes the area reading. Either way the ditch is large, and it is filled with water (18:35).
orig: כְּבֵית סָאתַיִם זֶרַע (kevet sa'tayim zera'), "like a house of two seahs of seed"

a: Get four jars filled with water
p: Where did Elijah get twelve jars of water after three dry years? Readers have answered in different ways.
b: The sea lies below Carmel, and some springs on the mountain may still have flowed; Josephus says the water came from a spring. The point of the pouring is plain: no hidden fire, and no one can say the wood caught by accident. A Jewish legend, gathered by Louis Ginzberg, says the prophets of Baal had hidden a man inside their altar to light it, and that he died there. Christian writers saw a picture of baptism in the water and the fire. The repeated pouring, three times, builds the suspense before the answer.

a: LORD, God of Abraham, Isaac and Israel
p: Elijah calls on the God of the patriarchs, the name God gave Moses at the burning bush.
b: At Horeb God told Moses, "I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob" (Exodus 3:6). Elijah uses the same form but says "Israel" instead of "Jacob," echoing the twelve stones and the name "Israel will be your name" (18:31). His three requests, that it be known that the LORD is God, that Elijah is his servant, and that he has acted at God's word, put the whole contest on God's credit, not his own.

a: you yourself have turned their hearts backward
p: Elijah says God "turned their hearts backward." Is God turning Israel back to himself, or did he let them turn away?
b: The verb is a perfect, "you have turned," and the line ends with achoranit, "backward." This translation keeps both words and leaves the sense open, because readers take it two ways. Many hear a confident prayer: the fire will show that God has turned the people back to himself. Others hear Elijah saying that God had let their hearts turn away from him. The Talmud takes it that way and calls the words bold, almost insolent (Bavli Berakhot 31b); compare Isaiah's "Why, LORD, do you make us stray from your ways?" (Isaiah 63:17). The words matter for later hope: Malachi says God will send Elijah to "turn the hearts" of parents and children (Malachi 4:6), and Luke applies this to John the Baptist (Luke 1:17).

a: Down came the LORD's fire
p: Fire from heaven marks the LORD's acceptance of a sacrifice, from the tabernacle to Solomon's temple.
b: When Aaron first sacrificed, "Fire came out from before the LORD and ate up the burnt offering" (Leviticus 9:24). Fire also consumes Gideon's offering (Judges 6:21), David's (1 Chronicles 21:26) and Solomon's (2 Chronicles 7:1). Elijah later calls fire down on soldiers (2 Kings 1:10–12), and two of Jesus' disciples want to do the same; in many later manuscripts they add "as Elijah did," and Jesus rebukes them (Luke 9:54–55). Revelation warns that a false prophet will also make fire come down (Revelation 13:13), so fire alone does not prove truth.
r: Leviticus 9:24; Judges 6:21; 1 Chronicles 21:26; 2 Kings 1:10–12; Luke 9:54–55; Revelation 13:13

a: The LORD, he is the God!
t: Said at the end of Yom Kippur
p: The people's cry closes the holiest day of the Jewish year, repeated seven times.
b: "Adonai hu ha-Elohim," "the LORD, he is the God," is the climax of the chapter and of Elijah's name, which says the same thing (17:1). At the close of the Day of Atonement, in the service called Ne'ilah, the congregation repeats it seven times, after the Shema and "Blessed be the name...". Moses had said, "the LORD is God. Apart from him there is no other" (Deuteronomy 4:35). This passage (18:1–39) is also read in synagogues as the prophetic reading paired with the golden calf story (Exodus 32), another day when Israel had to choose.

a: the Kishon River
p: The Kishon runs along the foot of Carmel to the sea. Deborah's victory over Sisera was won on its banks.
b: The Kishon drains the Jezreel Valley and flows northwest under the Carmel ridge to the bay of Haifa. In the Song of Deborah, "The Kishon River swept them away" (Judges 5:21), when the LORD sent rain on Sisera's chariots. The place of slaughter thus recalls an old victory of the LORD of the storm over the Canaanites. The traditional site of the contest at el-Muhraqa overlooks the Kishon valley. The Hebrew calls both the Kerith (17:3) and the Kishon a nachal, a stream bed that can run dry; this translation says "brook" for the small Kerith and "River" for the Kishon, as the Plain English of Judges does.

a: slaughtered them there
p: Elijah has the prophets of Baal killed. Readers have defended, explained and questioned it.
b: Deuteronomy commands death for a prophet who leads Israel after other gods: "That prophet or that dreamer of dreams must be put to death" (Deuteronomy 13:5; see Deuteronomy 17:2–7), and the story assumes that law. Jezebel had killed the LORD's prophets first (18:4), and Moses' Levites (Exodus 32:26–28) and Phinehas (Numbers 25:11) acted in the same zeal. Many Jewish and Christian readers have read the scene as just judgment in Israel's covenant setting, not a pattern for today. No command from God for the killing is recorded: Elijah gives the order himself, though at the altar he had said he acted "because you told me to" (18:36), and many readers build on that silence. Others are troubled: the rabbis say Elijah defended the Father's honor but not the son's, Israel's (Mekhilta, Pisha 1), and Jesus refuses fire on a Samaritan village (Luke 9:54–55). Critical scholars note that the story may come from later writers fighting Baal worship in words.

a: with his face between his knees
p: Elijah crouches with his head between his knees. The Talmud tells of a later holy man who prayed the same way.
b: The narrator does not say Elijah prayed, but James reads the scene as prayer: "he prayed once more, and the sky gave rain" (James 5:18). The posture may be one of intense prayer or of deep humility. The Talmud tells that Hanina ben Dosa, a first-century wonder-worker, "put his head between his knees" and prayed for the sick son of Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai, who then recovered (Bavli Berakhot 34b). The contrast with the prophets of Baal is sharp: they shouted and gashed themselves; Elijah crouches in silence.

a: a little cloud, like a person's hand, coming up out of the sea
p: Israel's rain comes in from the Mediterranean, to the west. A small cloud there could mean a coming storm.
b: The winter rains of the land of Israel come off the Mediterranean with westerly winds; Jesus says, "Whenever you see a cloud coming up over the west, you say right away, 'Rain is on its way'" (Luke 12:54). From the top of Carmel the servant can see far out over the sea. The tiny cloud "like a person's hand" has passed into English as a phrase for a small beginning of something great.

a: The LORD's hand was on Elijah
p: "The hand of the LORD" means God's power taking hold of a prophet. Elijah runs about 17 miles to Jezreel.
b: The idiom marks moments when God's power comes on a prophet: Elisha prophesies when "the hand of the LORD" comes on him (2 Kings 3:15), and Ezekiel's visions begin the same way (Ezekiel 1:3). Here it gives Elijah the strength to run ahead of a chariot from Carmel to Jezreel, about 17 miles (27 km), in a downpour. Running before the king's chariot was the role of a royal herald (1 Samuel 8:11; 2 Samuel 15:1). For one day the prophet escorts the king home, as if the contest had won Ahab back.

a: The gods do this to me, and more besides
p: Jezebel uses Israel's usual curse formula, but with "gods" and a plural verb: she swears by Baal's gods, not the LORD.
b: The oath "God do this to me, and more besides" is common in Samuel and Kings (2 Samuel 19:13; 2:23). The speaker calls a curse down on himself if he fails. When an Israelite says it, elohim takes a singular verb and means God. Jezebel uses a plural verb, so it means "the gods," as when Ben-hadad swears (20:10). After the fire on Carmel, she answers not with fear but with a death threat, and gives Elijah a day's head start, perhaps because she wants him gone more than she wants him dead.
orig: כֹּה־יַעֲשׂוּן אֱלֹהִים (koh-ya'asun elohim), "so may the gods do"

a: Beersheba, the one in Judah
p: Beersheba was Judah's far southern town. By going there Elijah leaves Ahab's realm entirely.
b: "From Dan to Beersheba" was the standard way of saying "the whole land" (Judges 20:1; 2 Samuel 24:2). Beersheba lies about 100 miles (160 km) south of Jezreel, in the kingdom of Jehoshaphat. The note "the one in Judah" reminds a northern reader that the prophet has crossed a border. Beersheba also carries memories of Abraham, Hagar and Isaac (Genesis 21:14–33; Genesis 26:23–25), and Hagar's son also lies down under a bush in the wilderness near Beersheba to die (Genesis 21:14–16). Leaving his servant there, Elijah goes on alone.

a: a lone broom bush
p: The rotem is the white broom of the desert, a shrub that gives thin shade and burns into hot coals.
b: Rotem is the white broom (Retama raetam), a bush up to ten feet tall common in the Negev and Sinai. Its shade is thin, but it is often the only shade there is. Its roots were used for fuel and made long-lasting coals (Psalm 120:4), and the poor dug them up in famine (Job 30:4). Older Bibles call it a "juniper." The hot loaf the angel brings in 19:6 is baked on coals, perhaps from the same kind of bush.

a: Now, LORD, take my life.
p: Elijah joins Moses and Jonah, prophets who asked God to take their lives.
b: Moses, worn out by the people's complaints, said, "kill me, please, kill me outright" (Numbers 11:15). Jonah twice asks to die, once after Nineveh is spared and once under a withered plant (Jonah 4:3; Jonah 4:8). Job and Jeremiah curse the day they were born (Job 3:1–3; Jeremiah 20:14–18). Many readers today see in Elijah the signs of exhaustion and depression after a great high, and notice how God answers: not with a lecture but with sleep, food and a second meal. Elijah asks God to take his life; he does not take it himself.

a: I am not any better than my fathers
p: Elijah's words may mean that he has failed like the prophets before him, or simply that he too must die.
b: Some readers take "my fathers" to be the prophets before him: he hoped to end Baal worship and has failed like them. Others take it as ancestors in general: why should he live on when they did not? Still others hear wounded pride: he thought Carmel would make him greater than those before him. The sentence also prepares for the coming irony: Elijah, who here asks to die, is one of only two people in the Bible taken up without dying (2 Kings 2:11; Genesis 5:24).

a: an angel
p: Mal'akh means "messenger." In 19:7 he is called the LORD's angel.
b: The Hebrew mal'akh can be a human messenger, like Jezebel's (19:2, the same word), or a heavenly one. Here the same word that brought the queen's death threat brings God's food. In 19:7 he is "the LORD's angel," the figure who meets Hagar in the wilderness (Genesis 16:7), calls to Moses from the bush (Exodus 3:2) and later commands Elijah again (2 Kings 1:3, 2 Kings 1:15). Some readers identify the angel of the LORD with God himself; others see a messenger who speaks for God.

a: a round loaf baked on coals, and a jug of water
t: The widow's loaf and jug again
p: The words for the loaf and the jug are those of the widow's story. Elijah, who was fed by a widow, is fed by an angel.
b: In Zarephath Elijah asked the widow for a small round loaf ('uggah) and saw her jug (tsappachat) of oil that did not run dry (17:12–16). Now, at his lowest, a round loaf and a jug of water appear by his head. The repetition seems designed: the prophet who carried God's care to a starving widow now receives the same care himself. Christian readers have often seen in this meal a picture of the Lord's Supper, food for a journey; Jewish readers note that the same God who fed Israel in the wilderness with manna feeds his prophet on the way to the same mountain.

a: forty days and forty nights
p: Elijah's forty days repeat Moses' forty days on the mountain. Jesus' forty days in the wilderness echo both.
b: From Beersheba to the traditional site of Sinai is about 200 miles (320 km), a walk of perhaps two weeks. The forty days are less a travel time than a sign. Moses "stayed on the mountain forty days and forty nights" (Exodus 24:18), and on the second stay "Bread he did not eat, and water he did not drink" (Exodus 34:28). Israel wandered forty years. Jesus fasts forty days in the wilderness before his ministry (Matthew 4:2). Elijah, the prophet who renews the covenant, retraces the path of the one who received it.

a: God's mountain, Horeb
p: Horeb is Deuteronomy's name for Mount Sinai. Its location is still debated.
b: Exodus uses both names; Deuteronomy calls the mountain Horeb (Deuteronomy 5:2). This is the only time in the Old Testament that anyone after Moses returns there. The traditional site, Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai Peninsula, goes back to Christian monks of the fourth century; other proposals include mountains in northwest Arabia (in ancient Midian) and in the northern Sinai. Elijah's journey shows that in his day people still knew where to go, though the text does not say where it was.

a: He went into the cave there
p: The Hebrew says "the cave," as if a known one. Jewish tradition took it as the cleft where Moses saw God pass.
b: The definite article is unexpected for a place not mentioned before. Many readers think it points to the "crack in the rock" where God set Moses while his glory passed by (Exodus 33:22). The Talmud lists "the cave where Moses and Elijah stood" among the things God made at twilight on the eve of the first Sabbath (Bavli Pesahim 54a). Others take "the cave" as a general way of speaking, "a cave there." Either way, the next verses deliberately echo Exodus 33–34.

a: "Why are you here, Elijah?"
p: God's question can be heard as a rebuke, an invitation, or both. It is asked twice, before and after the vision.
b: The Hebrew is short: "What to you here, Elijah?" Some readers hear reproach: you were sent to Israel, not to the desert. Others hear the gentle question of God to Adam, "Where are you?" (Genesis 3:9), which invites a confession rather than demanding one. The question is repeated word for word after the wind, quake, fire and silence (19:13), and Elijah's answer does not change at all (19:14). That repetition is the key to the scene.

a: I have burned with zeal for the LORD
p: Elijah's "zealous, I have been zealous" uses the word for jealous love, the word of Phinehas and of God himself.
b: The Hebrew doubles the verb for emphasis: qanno' qinne'ti. The root qana' means jealousy in the sense of fierce, exclusive devotion; the LORD calls himself "jealous" (Exodus 20:5; Exodus 34:14). It is the word used of Phinehas, who "was zealous with my zeal among them" (Numbers 25:11). Jewish tradition identified Elijah with Phinehas, the zealous priest who never died (Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 47; Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Exodus 6:18). Later Jewish "zealots" claimed both as models (1 Maccabees 2:26, 2:58).
orig: קַנֹּא קִנֵּאתִי (qanno' qinne'ti), "I have been very zealous"

a: The Israelites have left your covenant behind
p: A midrash says that because Elijah charged Israel with leaving the covenant, he must attend every circumcision.
b: A midrash says Elijah's complaint was about the covenant of circumcision, which he claimed Israel had abandoned. God answered: by your life, Israel will never perform this covenant without you there to see it (Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 29). So at a Jewish circumcision (brit milah) a chair is set for Elijah, "the angel of the covenant" (Malachi 3:1), and the baby is placed on it before the rite. The legend turns Elijah's harsh charge into an honor that keeps proving him wrong.

a: the LORD was passing by
t: God passes by, as for Moses
p: "Passing by" is the verb of Exodus 33–34, where the LORD passes before Moses in the cleft of the rock.
b: When Moses asked to see God's glory, the LORD said, "I will make all my goodness pass in front of you" (Exodus 33:19), and later "The LORD passed in front of him and called out" his name (Exodus 34:6). Elijah stands at the same mountain, perhaps at the same cave, and the same verb, 'avar, is used. But where Moses heard the proclamation of God's mercy, Elijah first meets wind, quake and fire. The Hebrew is unclear whether "the LORD was passing by" is part of God's command ("for the LORD is about to pass") or the narrator's report.

a: The LORD was not in the wind.
t: Not in the wind, quake or fire
p: Wind, earthquake and fire were the signs of God's coming at Sinai. Here God is not in them.
b: At Sinai the mountain smoked and quaked because "the LORD had come down upon it in the fire" (Exodus 19:18), and the psalms describe the LORD coming in storm and earthquake (Psalm 18:7–15; Psalm 29). Baal too was a god of the storm. So the threefold "not" is striking. Readers explain it in different ways: God is free from the forces of nature and not to be identified with them; God's way with Elijah will now be quiet, not spectacular; or Carmel's fire, which Elijah wanted to repeat, is not how God will win Israel. The text does not say God was never in fire; it says he was not this time.

a: And after the fire
t: Claude's theory: the silence answers Carmel
p: Claude's theory: "no sound" was Baal's failure on Carmel; at Horeb the LORD comes as a sound that is silence.
b: This is my own reading, though it overlaps with many literary studies. On Carmel the narrator says twice of Baal, "Not a sound" (18:26, 18:29), using the same word qol. The LORD answered there with fire. At Horeb the order is reversed: fire comes, and the LORD is not in it; then comes a qol, a sound, made of silence. I suggest the story wants the reader to set the two scenes side by side. The dead god gives no sound; the living God can choose to come in a sound that is almost no sound. The lesson for Elijah, who keeps asking for fire (19:10; 2 Kings 1:10), would be that God's victory does not depend on spectacle.

a: a sound of thin silence
p: Qol is "sound" or "voice"; demamah, "silence"; daqqah, "thin." Each translation chooses a meaning.
b: Qol can be a voice or any sound. Demamah means stillness or silence: a storm turned to calm (Psalm 107:29), or the hush before a voice in Job 4:16. Daqqah means thin or fine, like manna fine as frost (Exodus 16:14) or dust (Isaiah 40:15). The readings: "a still small voice" (KJV), an inner, gentle word; "a gentle whisper" or "low whisper" (many modern Bibles); "a light breeze" (the Greek phōnē auras leptēs and the Latin "whistling of a gentle breeze"); "the sound of those who praise in silence," angels (Targum); and "a sound of thin silence" or "sheer silence" (literal renderings, the NRSV, many scholars). A minority (Johan Lust) argued for a roaring sound. This translation keeps "a sound of thin silence": it is closest to the words, keeps the paradox, and does not add a voice before 19:13.

a: he covered his face with his cloak
p: Like Moses at the bush, Elijah hides his face. The cloak he uses will pass to Elisha.
b: At the same mountain, "Moses covered his face, for he was afraid to gaze at God" (Exodus 3:6), and God told him, "no human being can see me and stay alive" (Exodus 33:20). Elijah's gesture shows that he knows he is in God's presence. The cloak ('adderet), a prophet's hairy mantle (2 Kings 1:8; Zechariah 13:4), will be thrown on Elisha (19:19), will part the Jordan (2 Kings 2:8) and will fall to Elisha when Elijah is taken up (2 Kings 2:13–14).

a: I have burned with zeal for the LORD
p: After the wind, quake, fire and silence, Elijah gives exactly the same answer, word for word.
b: Elijah's reply in 19:14 repeats 19:10 exactly in Hebrew. Readers take this in two main ways. Some see a faithful prophet stating the truth twice, and God answering with a plan and with seven thousand faithful (19:15–18). Others read it as a sign that Elijah has not been moved by the vision: he still sees himself as the only one left, and God's answer includes appointing a successor "to take your place" (19:16). Some Jewish legends criticize Elijah for accusing Israel instead of pleading for it (see the collection of Louis Ginzberg), while Paul reads the complaint as an "pleads with God against Israel" (Romans 11:2).

a: anoint Hazael as king over Aram
p: Hazael became king of Damascus about 842 BC. An Assyrian text calls him "son of a nobody," a usurper.
b: Shalmaneser III of Assyria fought "Hazael of Damascus" in 841 and 838 BC, and one of his inscriptions calls him the "son of a nobody," meaning he had no royal father; it says Hadadezer died and Hazael seized the throne. The Bible tells the same story from the other side: Elisha weeps before Hazael, who then smothers Ben-hadad (2 Kings 8:7–15). The Tel Dan Stele, found in 1993–94, is most likely Hazael's victory monument and mentions the "house of David." Elijah never anoints Hazael; Elisha, his successor, carries out the order in a strange way, by telling Hazael he will be king.

a: Jehu son of Nimshi
p: Jehu, the general who wiped out Ahab's house, is shown bowing before the king of Assyria.
b: Jehu seized the throne in about 841 BC, killing Ahab's son Joram and Jezebel (2 Kings 9–10). Here he is "son of Nimshi," but 2 Kings 9:2 and 9:14 call him son of Jehoshaphat son of Nimshi: Hebrew "son" can mean descendant, and Nimshi was probably the better-known name in the family. It is a son of the prophets, sent by Elisha, who anoints him (2 Kings 9:1–10). The Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III, now in the British Museum, shows "Jehu son of Omri" (that is, king of Omri's land) kneeling with his face to the ground and lists his tribute: the oldest surviving picture of an Israelite king. The Bible does not praise Jehu without limit: Hosea announces punishment for "the blood of Jezreel" that Jehu shed (Hosea 1:4).

a: you are to anoint as prophet
p: Kings and priests were anointed with oil. This is the only command to anoint a prophet.
b: Anointing with oil set apart kings (1 Samuel 10:1; 1 Samuel 16:13) and priests (Exodus 29:7). Prophets were not normally anointed, though Isaiah 61:1 speaks of being anointed by the Spirit, and Psalm 105:15 calls the patriarchs "my anointed ones... my prophets." When Elijah meets Elisha he uses no oil; he throws his cloak on him (19:19). Many readers take "anoint" here in the wider sense "appoint, consecrate."
orig: תִּמְשַׁח לְנָבִיא (timshach lenavi'), "you will anoint as prophet"

a: Whoever gets away from Hazael's sword, Jehu will kill.
p: God's answer to Elijah is a judgment carried out over a generation by a foreign king, a rebel general and a prophet.
b: Hazael's wars wasted Israel (2 Kings 8:12; 2 Kings 10:32–33), and Jehu killed Ahab's family and the worshipers of Baal (2 Kings 10). Elisha is never said to kill with a sword; readers think of the curse on the boys of Bethel (2 Kings 2:24) or of his word that guided the others. The verse disturbs many readers, who see in it the violence of the age. Others stress that it answers Elijah's complaint that Baal's people were winning: the LORD's judgment is coming, but in God's time and by God's chosen means, not Elijah's.

a: every knee that has not bent to Baal, and every mouth that has not kissed him
p: Paul cites this verse, in wording of his own, to argue that God always keeps a faithful remnant.
b: Elijah thought he was alone; God counts seven thousand. Kissing an idol was an act of worship (Hosea 13:2; Job 31:27). Paul cites the verse in Romans 11:4 in his own words. He keeps the first person of the Hebrew, God speaking ("I have left for myself seven thousand men"), but puts it in the past tense. The Hebrew form vehish'arti is usually read as future, "I will leave," though it can be past; the Greek of 1 Kings has "you will leave," and has "worshiped" where the Hebrew has "kissed" (see the variant). Paul draws the lesson that now too a remnant remains, chosen by grace (Romans 11:5). He writes Baal with a feminine article, as some books of the Greek Old Testament do, probably because readers said aischynē, "shame," in place of the god's name.

a: Twelve pairs of oxen were ahead of him
p: Twelve teams of oxen mean a large farm. Elisha leaves real wealth to follow Elijah.
b: Plowing was done with a yoke of two oxen. Twelve pairs plowing in a line, with Elisha behind the last, suggest a large estate, either his family's or one where he worked. Abel-meholah lay in the Jordan valley, good farmland. The number twelve may also echo the twelve stones of Carmel (18:31). Elisha's call costs him: unlike Elijah, he does not come out of nowhere; he comes from a settled, prosperous home.

a: tossed his cloak onto him
p: Throwing a cloak over someone claimed him. Elisha understands at once.
b: No words are spoken. Elijah crosses over to Elisha and throws his cloak on him, and Elisha runs after him. Covering someone with a garment can mean claiming or protecting them: Ruth asks Boaz, "Spread the wing of your cloak over your servant" (Ruth 3:9). The prophet's cloak was his badge (2 Kings 1:8). The Greek calls it a mēlōtē, a sheepskin, and Hebrews 11:37 uses that word for the faithful who wandered in sheepskins, probably with Elijah in mind. The scene gave English the phrase "the mantle passes" for a handing on of leadership. Elisha will receive the cloak itself when Elijah is taken up (2 Kings 2:13).

a: What have I done to you?
t: "Go back. What have I done to you?"
p: Elijah's answer is unclear in Hebrew. Is he giving permission, testing Elisha, or rebuking him?
b: Literally: "Go, return, for what have I done to you?" Readers take it in three ways. (1) Permission: go, I have not bound you; do as you like. (2) Challenge: go back if you want, but think about what I have just done to you. (3) Rebuke: why delay, after what I did? Elisha's response, a farewell feast and then following, suits the first two best. Jesus seems to have this scene in mind when a would-be follower asks to say goodbye to his family first: no one who has laid his hand on a plow and keeps looking at what is behind is fit for God's kingdom (Luke 9:61–62). Jesus asks more than Elijah did.
orig: לֵךְ שׁוּב כִּי מֶה־עָשִׂיתִי לָךְ (lekh shuv ki meh-'asiti lakh)

a: With the oxen's gear for fuel
p: Elisha kills his oxen and burns their yokes: no way back to farming.
b: Elisha slaughters the pair of oxen as a sacrifice or a feast (zavach can mean either), cooks the meat over a fire made from the plowing gear, and gives it to the people. Readers see a farewell meal, a thank-offering, or a public sign that he will not return. Many sermons have called it "burning the plow." The phrase "waited on him" uses sharat, the word for Joshua as Moses' assistant (Exodus 24:13): Elisha begins as Elijah's servant, as Joshua began as Moses'. In 2 Kings he is called the one "the one who poured water over Elijah's hands" (2 Kings 3:11).

a: Ben-hadad, the king of Aram
p: Ben-hadad, "son of Hadad," was a throne name in Damascus. The Assyrian records name Ahab's neighbor differently.
b: Ben-hadad means "son of Hadad," the storm god of Aram, and several kings of Damascus bore it (15:18; 2 Kings 13:3). The Greek translation spells it "son of Hader." Here is a puzzle for historians: Assyrian inscriptions say that in 853 BC the king of Damascus was Hadadezer (Adad-idri), and that he fought beside Ahab, not against him (see the note on 22:1). Some, following J. Maxwell Miller, think the wars of chapters 20 and 22 were first told of a later "king of Israel" fighting Ben-hadad son of Hazael (2 Kings 13:24–25), and only later tied to Ahab; notice that the king is often unnamed. Others suggest Ben-hadad was Hadadezer's title or another name, or that the wars came before the alliance.

a: thirty-two kings
p: Ben-hadad's "kings" were probably rulers of small city-states and tribes under Damascus.
b: In Syria in this period "king" could mean the ruler of a single city or a tribal chief. The Assyrian account of Qarqar lists twelve kings in the alliance against Shalmaneser III, from Damascus and Hamath to Arabia and Egypt. Thirty-two subject rulers marching with Damascus is not impossible for a strong king. Their removal in 20:24, replaced by governors, may reflect a real reform: Aram moving from a league of allies to a state run by its own officers.

a: Your silver and gold belong to me
p: Ben-hadad's first demand asks Ahab to admit he is a vassal. The second means plunder.
b: Ahab accepts the first message at once (20:4), probably because it asks for words more than goods: a vassal says that all he has belongs to his overlord. The second message (20:5–6) makes it real: Ben-hadad's servants will search the palace and take what they like. Ahab then consults the elders, who tell him not to give in. Readers note that here Ahab acts as a careful king who seeks counsel, a different picture from the Ahab of the Elijah stories, which is one reason many think chapter 20 comes from a different source.

a: The man buckling his belt on should not brag like the man taking it off.
p: Four Hebrew words: "Let not the one girding boast like the one ungirding." Brag after the battle, not before.
b: The proverb is only four words in Hebrew. A soldier put on his belt, with sword and armor, before battle and took it off after. Boasting belongs to the man who has come home safe, not to the one still getting ready. Ahab answers Ben-hadad's brag about the dust of Samaria (20:10) with the wit of a man who has nothing else to fight with yet. Proverbs gives the same advice: don't brag about tomorrow, since you do not know what a day will bring (Proverbs 27:1).

a: in the shelters
p: Sukkot means booths or shelters. Some scholars think it is the town of Succoth, east of the Jordan.
b: A sukkah is a shelter made of branches, used by armies in the field (2 Samuel 11:11). Most translations say Ben-hadad was drinking "in the tents" or "booths." Yigael Yadin proposed that it is the place-name Succoth in the Jordan Valley, where an army besieging Samaria might keep its base and supply line. The Hebrew spelling allows both. Either way the picture is the same: a king feasting while his enemy prepares.

a: a certain prophet
p: In chapter 20 unnamed prophets help Ahab win. Not every prophet in Kings is against the king.
b: After the Elijah chapters, readers may be surprised that a prophet now brings Ahab good news and battle plans (20:13–14, 20:22, 20:28). The LORD's reason is given: "you will know that I am the LORD." The help is for God's name, not as a reward for Ahab. Critical scholars think chapters 20 and 22 come from a different collection of prophetic war stories, where prophets advise kings in war, as Elisha does in 2 Kings 3 and 6. The chapter ends, however, with a prophet condemning Ahab (20:42), so the two pictures meet.

a: Then you will know that I am the LORD.
t: "You will know that I am the LORD"
p: The phrase from the exodus story, where the plagues teach Egypt who the LORD is.
b: The formula runs through the exodus: "Egypt will know that I am the LORD" (Exodus 7:5; see also Exodus 14:4). Ezekiel uses it more than fifty times. Here and in 20:28 it explains why God helps a king who worships Baal: the victory is meant to teach Israel, and Aram, who rules the hills and the valleys.

a: the young men of the district officials
p: The "young men" were probably picked soldiers or attendants of the district governors, only 232 of them.
b: Na'ar, "young man," also means a squire or trained retainer, like the young men of Abner and Joab (2 Samuel 2:14). The "district officials" (sarei hammedinot) governed the provinces of the kingdom. A few hundred such men lead the attack, with the seven thousand following (20:15). The point of the story is the small number against a vast army, as with Gideon's three hundred (Judges 7:2–7) and Jonathan and his armor-bearer (1 Samuel 14:6).

a: seven thousand
p: Israel's army numbers seven thousand, the same number as the faithful who did not bow to Baal (19:18).
b: The number may be a coincidence, but readers have long noticed it. In 19:18 the LORD says he will keep seven thousand in Israel who have not bent the knee to Baal; here the LORD wins a battle with an army of seven thousand. Some read the link as a hint that God's remnant fights for Israel; others think the number is a round one, used twice by different storytellers.

a: drinking himself drunk
p: The narrator mentions Ben-hadad's drinking twice. A king who is drunk at noon has already lost.
b: Ben-hadad receives the answer while drinking (20:12) and is drunk when the attack comes at midday (20:16). Proverbs warns that wine is not for kings, because it makes them forget the law (Proverbs 31:4–5). The story uses the detail for irony: the boasting king gives orders that cannot be carried out ("take them alive") while his army is cut to pieces. Compare Belshazzar's feast on the night of Babylon's fall (Daniel 5).

a: Their god is a god of the mountains.
p: Many ancient peoples thought a god's power was tied to a region. The LORD answers that he rules both.
b: The Aramean officers think like many of their neighbors: each land and landscape had its own gods (2 Kings 17:26; 2 Kings 5:17). Since Samaria stood on a hill, they reason that Israel's god is a mountain god. The LORD's reply (20:28) is the point of the chapter: he will give Aram into Israel's hand in the valley too, "and you will know that I am the LORD." Some scholars connect the old divine title El Shaddai with a word for mountain, but this is uncertain, and the officers' theory does not depend on it. Verdict: a real ancient belief, quoted to be refuted.

a: Their god is a god of the mountains.
t: God or gods of the mountains?
p: The Hebrew elohim can mean "god" or "gods." Foreign speakers might mean either.
b: The Arameans say elohei harim elohehem, which can mean "their god is a god of mountains" or "their gods are gods of mountains," as the KJV and many others have it. No verb shows the number. Foreign speakers often use the plural (see the note on Jezebel's oath at 19:2), which favors "gods." But in 20:28 the LORD quotes them as speaking of one god, "the LORD is a god of mountains," so this translation uses the singular here to match. Either way the Arameans think of Israel's God as one local power among many, tied to the hill country; the battle in the plain will prove otherwise.

a: Aphek
p: Several towns were called Aphek. This one was probably east of the Sea of Galilee, on the road to Damascus.
b: Aphek means "stronghold" or "riverbed" and was a common place name. The Aphek of the Philistine wars lay on the coastal plain (1 Samuel 4:1). This one, where Aram fights "on flat ground," is usually located on the plateau east of the Sea of Galilee, near the modern village of Fiq or En Gev, on the main road from Damascus to Israel. Elisha later promises King Joash a victory over Aram at Aphek (2 Kings 13:17).

a: a hundred thousand
p: A hundred thousand dead in one day, and a wall falling on twenty-seven thousand: how should readers take these numbers?
b: The numbers in this chapter are very large for armies of the ninth century; at Qarqar the whole Syrian alliance is said to have fielded around fifty thousand foot soldiers. Some readers take them at face value. Others note that the Hebrew 'elef, "thousand," can also mean a military unit or clan (Judges 6:15; 1 Samuel 10:19), so "a hundred units" would be far fewer men. Others again see round, heroic numbers in the style of war stories, meant to say "a total defeat." The fall of Aphek's wall also recalls Jericho (Joshua 6:20).

a: a room inside a room
p: The Hebrew idiom for an inner, hidden room. Micaiah will use it again of Zedekiah.
b: Cheder becheder, "a room in a room," means a back room, as far from the door as one can get. Ben-hadad hides there after his defeat. Micaiah later tells the false prophet Zedekiah that he will see the truth "when you go into a room inside a room to hide" (22:25). The repeated phrase links the two defeated men.

a: kings who show loyal love
p: Many Bibles say "merciful kings." The Hebrew hesed is loyal love: faithfulness to a bond or treaty.
b: The servants of Ben-hadad call Israel's kings malkhei chesed. Hesed, rendered "loyal love" on this site, is kindness that keeps faith with a relationship. Here it likely means that Israel's kings honored treaties and spared those who surrendered. The phrase is ironic: Ahab shows hesed to the enemy whom God had handed to him, and is condemned for it (20:42). Readers debate whether Ahab's mercy was humane, politically wise, or disobedient; the prophet's verdict makes the narrator's view plain.
orig: מַלְכֵי חֶסֶד (malkhei chesed), "kings of loyal love"

a: tie sackcloth on our waists and put ropes on our heads
p: Sackcloth was the dress of mourning. Ropes may have marked them as prisoners ready to be led away.
b: Sackcloth, a rough goat-hair cloth, was worn in grief and repentance (21:27; Jonah 3:6). The ropes "on our heads" are less clear: perhaps cords around the neck, as captives were often shown in Assyrian reliefs, or a sign that they put their lives in the victor's hands. Either way the envoys come as men already defeated, asking only for life.

a: He is my brother.
p: In ancient diplomacy kings of equal rank called each other "brother." Ahab offers a treaty, not mercy alone.
b: In the Amarna letters (about 1350 BC) and other royal correspondence, kings of equal rank address each other as "my brother," while a vassal calls his master "my lord" (as Ahab did in 20:4). By calling Ben-hadad "my brother," Ahab raises his defeated enemy to equal status. The envoys, watching for a sign, seize the word at once (20:33). Solomon and Hiram used the same language (9:13).

a: trading streets for yourself in Damascus
p: Ben-hadad offers Israel a trading quarter in his capital, as Aram had held one in Samaria.
b: Chutsot, literally "outside places" or "streets," here means bazaars or a merchants' quarter. Ancient states often kept trading colonies in each other's cities; Assyrian merchants had them in Anatolia centuries earlier. The Bible records no Aramean conquest from Omri; 15:20 tells of an earlier Ben-hadad taking towns from Baasha, so "my father ... your father" may be used loosely of each king's predecessors, one more puzzle of chapter 20. The return of towns and the trade rights show this was a real treaty, a "covenant." Historians link it with the fact that, at Qarqar in 853 BC, Ahab and the king of Damascus fought side by side against Assyria.

a: the sons of the prophets
p: Not the children of prophets, but members of a prophetic group or guild.
b: "Son of" in Hebrew can mean "member of a group." The bene hannevi'im appear here for the first time and often in the Elisha stories (2 Kings 2:3–7; 2 Kings 4:38; 2 Kings 6:1). They lived in communities at Bethel, Jericho and Gilgal, ate together and looked to a leader. Amos says, "I am no prophet, and I am no prophet's son" (Amos 7:14), meaning he did not belong to such a group. The nameless prophet here acts on his own initiative but "at the LORD's command."

a: the lion will kill you
t: Killed for refusing a strange order
p: A man who would not strike a prophet is killed by a lion. Readers find the story hard.
b: The punishment seems out of all proportion, and many readers say so. The story is told to make one point: a word from the LORD, however odd, must be obeyed, and the king who will not obey (20:42) stands condemned by the same rule. A similar lion kills the man of God from Judah who disobeyed (13:24). Some readers see here the narrator's harsh view of prophetic authority; others treat the lion stories as a teaching form, like a parable, more than a record.

a: a bandage over his eyes
p: The KJV says "ashes upon his face." The Hebrew 'apher is a headband or bandage, as 20:41 shows.
b: The KJV read the word as 'efer, "ashes," and pictured a mourner. But in 20:41 the prophet "took the bandage away from his eyes," which fits a cloth, not ash. The word 'apher appears only here and in 20:41, and modern dictionaries take it as a headband or bandage. A wounded soldier with his head bound would look exactly like the man in his story, and the bandage also hides his face from the king, who may know him.

a: a talent of silver
p: A talent was about 75 pounds (34 kg) of silver: a fortune no common soldier could pay.
b: The talent was the largest weight, sixty minas or three thousand shekels, roughly 75 pounds of silver. Omri bought the whole hill of Samaria for two talents (16:24). The choice offered, a life or a talent, is no real choice for a soldier: it means death. That makes the king's verdict in 20:40 all the harsher, and it sets up the prophet's reply, "your life will go for his life" (20:42).

a: So that is your verdict. You have settled it yourself.
p: Like Nathan with David, the prophet tells a case and lets the king pass sentence on himself.
b: The method is Nathan's: David heard about the rich man who took a poor man's lamb and said, "the man who did this deserves death!" Then Nathan said, "You are the man!" (2 Samuel 12:5–7). The wise woman of Tekoa did the same (2 Samuel 14:1–20). Ahab, judging the soldier who let a prisoner slip, has judged himself for letting Ben-hadad go. Scholars call these "judicial parables."

a: the man I put under the ban
p: Cherem means devoted to destruction, given wholly to God. Ahab, like Saul, spared what God had claimed.
b: "My man of cherem" means a man the LORD had devoted to destruction. The ban is the rule of holy war (Deuteronomy 7:2; Deuteronomy 20:16–17), and the parallel with Saul is close: Saul spared Agag king of Amalek and the best of the spoil, and "Those they would not put under the ban" (1 Samuel 15:9), and lost his kingdom. Nothing earlier in the chapter tells Ahab that Ben-hadad was under the ban, which troubles some readers; the narrator assumes the victory itself, given by the LORD, made the captive God's.

a: sulking and fuming
p: The same two words describe Ahab after Naboth refuses him (21:4).
b: Sar veza'ef, "resentful and raging," is Ahab's mood twice: here after the prophet's verdict and in 21:4 after Naboth's refusal. In the Hebrew order the two scenes stand side by side, and the repetition links them: a king who does not get his way sulks. In the Greek order, where the Naboth story comes earlier (see the variant at 21:1), the link runs the other way.

a: Naboth the Jezreelite
p: Jezreel was the Omride kings' residence in the fertile valley. Excavations have found a large royal compound.
b: Samaria was the capital, but the kings of Omri's house also kept a palace at Jezreel, at the eastern end of the Jezreel Valley, on the road to the Jordan (18:45–46). Excavations by David Ussishkin and John Woodhead in the 1990s found a large walled enclosure with towers, dated by many to the ninth century. Rock-cut wine presses in the area show that it was vineyard country. In the Hebrew, Naboth's family plot lay in Jezreel, right beside the palace, which is why the king wanted it. The Greek has no "in Jezreel" and puts the vineyard beside the "threshing floor" of Ahab king of Samaria (see the variant), which some scholars take as a sign that the story was once set at Samaria (see the note on 21:19). Ahab is called here "king of Samaria," an unusual title, perhaps to stress that he did not belong in Jezreel.

a: a garden of greens
t: A vineyard turned into a vegetable patch
p: Deuteronomy calls Egypt a land watered "like a vegetable garden." Ahab wants to turn an Israelite vineyard into one.
b: The phrase gan yaraq, "garden of greens," appears elsewhere only in Deuteronomy, where Egypt is the land where "you planted your seed and watered it with your foot, like a vegetable garden" (Deuteronomy 11:10). Some readers see a deliberate echo: the king wants to make the promised land like Egypt, the house of slavery. The vineyard is also an old picture of Israel itself (Isaiah 5:1–7). Others think the phrase is simply practical: a palace garden next door.

a: my fathers' inheritance
p: Naboth is not being stubborn. The Law treated family land as the LORD's gift, not to be sold for good.
b: Nachalah, "inheritance," is the land given to each family when Israel entered Canaan. The Law said: "The land must not be sold for good, because the land is mine" (Leviticus 25:23), and "Every Israelite must keep the inheritance of his fathers' tribe" (Numbers 36:7). A plot could be leased until the Jubilee but not given away. Naboth's oath, "The LORD keep me from" it, shows he sees the sale as sin. Ahab offers a fair price; the story presents Jezebel as seeing only a subject's refusal. Some scholars suggest she brought a Phoenician view of kingship, but we know little of Phoenician land law, and Samuel had warned that Israel's own king would take "Your fields, your vineyards and your olive groves" (1 Samuel 8:14).
orig: נַחֲלַת אֲבֹתַי (nachalat avotai), "the inheritance of my fathers"
r: Leviticus 25:23–28; Numbers 27:1–11; Numbers 36:7; 1 Samuel 8:14; Micah 2:2; Ezekiel 46:18

a: turned his face away, and would not eat a bite
p: Ahab lies on his bed facing the wall and refuses food, like a child. The narrator does not hide the comedy.
b: The great king who fought Ben-hadad now lies on his bed and will not eat because a farmer said no. Many readers find the picture comic and pathetic at once. Others note that Ahab, unlike his wife, at least accepts the refusal: he does not take the vineyard by force. Hezekiah also turns his face to the wall on his bed, but to pray (2 Kings 20:2). The contrast is often drawn.

a: Is that any way for you to rule as king over Israel?
p: Jezebel's words can be read as a question or as a mocking statement: "You are the king of Israel now!"
b: The Hebrew reads "You now, you do kingship over Israel." Without punctuation it can be a question ("Is this how you rule?") or a sarcastic statement ("Some king you are!"). Either way, Jezebel holds a view of kingship common in her world: a king takes what he wants. Israel's law limits the king, who must not lift himself above his brothers (Deuteronomy 17:20), and the prophets judge him by that law. Her "I myself will give you" mirrors Ahab's offer "I will give you" to Naboth (21:2): what he could not buy she will take.
orig: אַתָּה עַתָּה תַּעֲשֶׂה מְלוּכָה עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵל ('attah 'attah ta'aseh melukhah 'al-Yisra'el)

a: stamping them with his seal
t: The king's seal, and a seal of Jezebel?
p: Letters were closed with a clay sealing pressed by the owner's seal. A seal inscribed "Jezebel" is known.
b: A seal stamped into clay made a letter official, so Jezebel's letters carry the king's authority, used without his knowledge or with his silent consent. Thousands of seals and seal impressions survive from Iron Age Israel and Judah. In 1964 Nahman Avigad published a large stone seal, bought on the antiquities market, decorated with Egyptian and Phoenician symbols and inscribed yzbl, "Jezebel." Marjo Korpel later argued that it belonged to the queen; others think it was the seal of another woman of the same name, or are cautious because its origin is unknown.

a: Call for a fast
p: Public fasts were called in times of disaster to find and remove guilt. Jezebel uses one as a stage for a trial.
b: Israel fasted in crises: after defeat (Judges 20:26), in drought or locusts (Joel 1:14), or to turn away God's anger (Jonah 3:5). A fast implied that someone's sin was causing trouble, and in the famine of Elijah's time that would sound believable. Setting Naboth "at the head of the people" gives him a place of honor, or puts him where all can see him accused. The plan uses religious forms and legal rules to commit a murder.

a: two worthless men
p: Jezebel follows the letter of the law: two witnesses. The men are "sons of beliyya'al," worthless men.
b: The Law required more than one witness for a death sentence: "The one who is to die is to be put to death on the word of two witnesses or three witnesses" (Deuteronomy 17:6; see Deuteronomy 19:15). Jezebel provides two. They are bene beliyya'al, rendered on this site "worthless men," the phrase used of the men of Gibeah (Judges 19:22). The Law also forbade false testimony (Exodus 20:16) and laid the punishment of the crime on a lying witness (Deuteronomy 19:18–19). The gospels tell of false witnesses at Jesus' trial (Mark 14:55–59), and Acts of those who accused Stephen (Acts 6:11–13).

a: You have cursed God and the king!
p: The Hebrew says "blessed." Scribes avoided writing "cursed God" and wrote "blessed" instead.
b: The verb is berakhta, "you blessed." Hebrew writers used "bless" in place of "curse" when God was the object, to avoid putting the words "curse God" on the page; Job's wife says "bless God and die" (Job 2:9; see Job 1:5, 1:11). Every major translation rightly renders "cursed." The charge fits the Law: "Do not treat God with contempt, and do not curse a leader of your people" (Exodus 22:28), and blasphemy was punished by stoning (Leviticus 24:16). By adding "the king," the charge also made Naboth a traitor.
orig: בֵּרַכְתָּ אֱלֹהִים וָמֶלֶךְ (berakhta Elohim vamelekh), "you blessed God and king"

a: stoned him with stones, and he died
p: 2 Kings adds that Naboth's sons were killed too, which would leave no heir to claim the land.
b: Jehu later recalls "the blood of Naboth and the blood of his sons" (2 Kings 9:26). If the sons died with their father, no heir was left, and the land could pass to the crown. The Talmud discusses whether the property of a man executed by the king goes to the king, and uses Naboth as its example (Bavli Sanhedrin 48b). Stoning took place outside the town (Leviticus 24:14; Acts 7:58), so that the town would not be made unclean by the death.

a: Take possession of
p: The word of the conquest: Israel was to take possession of Canaan. Ahab takes possession of an Israelite's land.
b: Yarash, "take possession of," is used four times in this chapter (21:15, 21:16, 21:18, 21:19). In Deuteronomy and Joshua it is the verb for taking the land from the nations the LORD drove out (Deuteronomy 1:8). Ahab uses it against one of God's own people, and Elijah throws it back in his face: "Have you murdered, and taken possession as well?" (21:19). Verse 21:26 adds that Ahab behaved like the Amorites whom the LORD drove out, using the same root.

a: Have you murdered, and taken possession as well?
p: Two Hebrew words, ratsachta vegam-yarashta. Ahab has broken the commandments against murder and craving.
b: Elijah's charge is two verbs: "you murdered, and also took possession." The commandments said, "You must not murder" (Exodus 20:13) and "You must not crave your neighbor's house" (Exodus 20:17). Ahab craved, Jezebel arranged false witness and murder, and Ahab took the field. Christian readers have often used the story as an illustration of James 4:2: you want something and do not get it, so you kill. Jewish readers note that the prophet holds the king responsible even though the queen did the plotting.

a: Right where the dogs licked up Naboth's blood
t: Where did the dogs lick Ahab's blood?
p: Elijah says "right where" Naboth died. Naboth died at Jezreel, but Ahab's blood is licked up at Samaria.
