b: In the Hebrew, Naboth is stoned outside the town (21:13), and the town is Jezreel (21:1); 2 Kings 9:25–26 also places his plot at Jezreel. Yet in 22:38 the dogs lick Ahab's blood at the pool of Samaria, "according to the word the LORD had spoken." Readers resolve this in three main ways. (1) "Right where" means "in the same way," or "in return for" (some take bimqom asher in that sense). (2) In an older form of the story Naboth died at Samaria: the Greek of 21:1 lacks "in Jezreel" and puts the vineyard by the threshing floor of the king of Samaria (see the variant there), and the Greek of 21:19 and 22:38 adds pigs at both places, tying the scenes together. (3) 21:29 moved the exact fulfillment to Ahab's son Joram, whose body Jehu throws onto Naboth's plot (2 Kings 9:25–26). Critical scholars think two traditions about the end of Ahab's house were joined.

a: You've found me, have you, my enemy?
p: Ahab calls Elijah his enemy. Elijah's "I have found you" answers that sin has found Ahab out.
b: Ahab's greeting is close to the one on Carmel, "the one who brings trouble on Israel" (18:17). He sees the prophet as a political opponent. Elijah takes up his verb: "I have found you," as if to say that Ahab's sin has found him out (compare Numbers 32:23). The reason is in the next words: Ahab "sold" himself, like a slave, to do evil. Readers note how quickly Ahab knows why the prophet has come; his conscience is already awake.

a: you sold yourself
p: To "sell oneself" is to become someone's slave. Ahab has made himself a slave to doing evil.
b: The verb hitmakker, "sell oneself," is used of Israelites offering themselves for sale as slaves (Deuteronomy 28:68); a related form describes a poor Israelite sold into service (Leviticus 25:39). Applied to Ahab, it means he has given himself over completely. The same is said of Israel before its fall (2 Kings 17:17). Paul uses a similar picture: "sold under sin" (Romans 7:14). Verse 21:25 repeats the charge and adds that Jezebel pushed him into it.

a: every male of Ahab's, the bound and the free
p: "Every male" is literally "every one who urinates against a wall." "The bound and the free" is unclear.
b: The first idiom, mashtin beqir, appears in judgments on ruling houses (14:10; 16:11; 2 Kings 9:8) and in David's oath about Nabal (1 Samuel 25:22). The KJV kept it literally. It simply means every male. The second, 'atsur ve'azuv, "held back and left," is debated: "slave and free," "minors and adults," "married and single," or "protected and unprotected." Whatever its exact sense, the pair means "everyone, without exception." Elijah's words here repeat the doom spoken on the houses of Jeroboam (14:10) and Baasha (16:3–4).
orig: מַשְׁתִּין בְּקִיר עָצוּר וְעָזוּב (mashtin beqir 'atsur ve'azuv)

a: The dogs will eat Jezebel
p: The prophecy is fulfilled in 2 Kings 9, when Jehu has Jezebel thrown from a window.
b: When Jehu came to Jezreel, Jezebel painted her eyes and met him at a window with a taunt; at his word her servants threw her down, and when men went to bury her they found only her skull, feet and hands (2 Kings 9:30–37). Jehu quoted Elijah's word. The dogs that eat the dead were the city's scavengers, and to be left for them was the worst disgrace in the ancient world (Jeremiah 22:19). Revelation later uses "Jezebel" as a name for a false teacher in Thyatira (Revelation 2:20).

a: with Jezebel his wife egging him on
p: The narrator says Jezebel stirred Ahab up. Readers ask how much of the blame is hers and how much his.
b: The verb hesattah, "she incited," is the word for luring someone into sin (Deuteronomy 13:6; Job 2:3). Kings gives Jezebel the blame for the murder plot and for much of Ahab's Baal worship, and later tradition made her a type of the wicked woman. Some modern readers, such as Phyllis Trible, point out how closely Jezebel and Elijah mirror each other, and that her portrait was drawn by her opponents; she was also a loyal wife, a devoted worshiper of her own gods and a capable ruler. Others reply that the text plainly condemns Ahab too: it is his evil, sold for, and his repentance that God answers (21:27–29). The Greek of 21:27 goes further and says Ahab put on sackcloth "on the day he struck down Naboth" (see the variant there).

a: the idols
p: The word for idols here may be a scornful name, related to a word for dung.
b: Gillulim is a favorite word of Ezekiel (about forty times) and appears in Kings for the worst kings (15:12; 2 Kings 17:12; 2 Kings 21:11). Its root may mean "round things," logs or blocks, and Jewish and Christian scholars have long heard a play on gelel, "dung": idols as lumps of filth. Translations say simply "idols." The word is a mark of contempt, not a description of what the images looked like.

a: the Amorites
p: Here "Amorites" means all the peoples of Canaan before Israel, whose sin was said to have cost them the land.
b: The Amorites were a real people of Syria and Mesopotamia in the second millennium BC, but in the Bible the name often stands for all the pre-Israelite inhabitants of Canaan. God told Abraham his descendants would return "for the guilt of the Amorites is not yet full" (Genesis 15:16). By comparing Ahab to them, the narrator implies that Israel could lose the land in the same way (2 Kings 17:7–8; 2 Kings 21:11).

a: walked about slowly and quietly
p: The Hebrew 'at means slowly or gently. The KJV's "went softly" is a fair picture.
b: 'At describes a slow, quiet pace, as of a mourner or someone humbled (Isaiah 8:6 uses it of gently flowing water). Ahab's grief is outward in every way: torn clothes, sackcloth on the skin, fasting, sleeping in sackcloth. Some readers suspect show; the LORD's answer in the next verses treats it as real.

a: Since he has humbled himself before me
p: The worst king of Israel humbles himself, and God delays the disaster. Readers find hope in this, and a problem.
b: God points out Ahab's humility to Elijah, as if Elijah needed to see it. The verb nikhna', "humbled himself," is the word of 2 Chronicles 7:14 and of Manasseh's repentance (2 Chronicles 33:12). Jewish and Christian teachers have used the verse to show that no one is beyond repentance; God's mercy reaches even Ahab. The problem is the delay: the disaster falls on his son's house instead. Some readers see here the old idea of family guilt (Exodus 34:7); others note that Ahab's son will walk in his father's ways (22:52) and so share his punishment, as Ezekiel 18 would insist.

a: Three years passed quietly
p: From here to the end of 2 Kings, the main Greek manuscript, Codex Vaticanus, carries a text revised toward the Hebrew.
b: Scholars since Henry St. John Thackeray (1907) and Dominique Barthélemy (1963) have shown that in some parts of Samuel–Kings the Greek of Codex Vaticanus, and so the standard Rahlfs edition, is not the original Septuagint but a revision, called kaige, that brought it closer to the Hebrew. One such section runs from 1 Kings 22 to the end of 2 Kings. Here the Lucianic (Antiochene) manuscripts are the better witness to the Old Greek. The Greek readings this site gives for chapter 22 are those of Codex Vaticanus as printed in Rahlfs' edition, that is, the kaige text; the Lucianic readings are not reported here.

a: with no war between Aram and Israel
t: Three years of peace, and Qarqar
p: The three quiet years may include 853 BC, when Ahab and the king of Damascus fought side by side against Assyria.
b: The Kurkh Monolith of Shalmaneser III places "Ahab the Israelite" beside Hadadezer of Damascus against Assyria at Qarqar in 853 BC (see the chapter 16 page for the inscription itself). The Bible does not mention Qarqar, but the treaty of 20:34 and the "three years" of peace fit it well. Many historians think Ahab died soon after, in 853 or 852 BC, once the alliance broke up.

a: Jehoshaphat king of Judah came down to the king of Israel
p: After fifty years of border war, Judah and Israel are allies. Chronicles says the alliance was sealed by marriage.
b: Asa of Judah and Baasha of Israel had fought (15:16–22). Under Jehoshaphat the two kingdoms make peace (22:44), and Jehoshaphat's son Jehoram marries a daughter of Ahab, Athaliah (2 Kings 8:18, 8:26). Chronicles opens its version of this story by saying Jehoshaphat "tied himself to Ahab by marriage" and that Ahab held a great feast for him and coaxed him into the war (2 Chronicles 18:1–2). Chronicles also judges the alliance: on his return the prophet Jehu son of Hanani asks him, "Is it the wicked you should be helping? Is it those who hate the LORD you should love?" (2 Chronicles 19:2).

a: Ramoth-gilead
p: "Heights of Gilead," a fortress town east of the Jordan, fought over by Israel and Aram for decades.
b: Ramoth-gilead was a city of refuge in Gad's land (Deuteronomy 4:43; Joshua 20:8) and the seat of one of Solomon's districts (4:13). It is usually placed at Tell Ramith near the modern border of Jordan and Syria. It controlled the King's Highway north to Damascus. Ahab dies fighting for it; his son Joram is wounded there, and Jehu is anointed there (2 Kings 8:28–9:6).

a: The Lord will hand it over to the king.
p: The four hundred say "the Lord" (Adonai), not "the LORD," and "the king" without saying which king.
b: The prophets do not use the name YHWH; they say Adonai, "the Lord," a title that could apply to any god (2 Chronicles 18:5 has "God"). Jehoshaphat notices and asks for a prophet "of the LORD" (22:7). Their promise is also vague: "will hand it over to the king." It does not say which king, and in the end Ramoth-gilead stays in the king of Aram's hand. Like the oracle at Delphi in Greek tradition, the words can come true either way. Later, in 22:12, they do use the LORD's name, perhaps for Jehoshaphat's sake.
orig: וְיִתֵּן אֲדֹנָי בְּיַד הַמֶּלֶךְ (veyitten Adonai beyad hammelekh)

a: Isn't there still a prophet of the LORD around here?
p: The Talmud explains: four hundred prophets saying the same words is itself a warning sign.
b: Jehoshaphat has just heard four hundred prophets agree. Why ask for another? The Talmud answers with a saying of the prophets' tradition: one message may come to many prophets, but no two prophets prophesy in the same words. Four hundred voices repeating one phrase suggested a script, not a revelation (Bavli Sanhedrin 89a). Modern readers make a similar point about group pressure: the court prophets are paid by the king (compare 18:19) and tell him what he wants. Jehoshaphat may simply be asking for a prophet of Israel's God by name.

a: But I hate him.
p: Ahab admits he hates the one prophet who tells him the truth. The narrator lets him condemn himself.
b: The king's honesty is almost comic: he knows a true prophet exists, and he hates him because he never says good things. Readers have pointed out the irony: Ahab knows that Micaiah's "evil" words come true, or he would not fear them. Jehoshaphat's mild reply, "The king shouldn't talk like that," sets up the scene. Isaiah describes a people who tell the seers not to see, and ask the prophets for smooth words (Isaiah 30:10).

a: a court official
p: A saris was a high court official. The word can mean eunuch, but often simply means officer.
b: Saris comes from an Assyrian title, "one who is at the king's head." Many such officers were eunuchs, and the word later means that; but Potiphar, who was married, is also a saris (Genesis 37:36). Here the sense is a royal attendant sent on an errand.

a: on the threshing floor at the opening of Samaria's gate
t: A threshing floor at the gate
p: Threshing floors were open public spaces, used for gatherings, judgment and, it seems, for seeking oracles.
b: A threshing floor was a flat, hard space where grain was beaten out; one near the city gate could hold a crowd. In the Ugaritic tale of Aqhat, King Danel sits "at the threshing floor by the gate" to judge the case of the widow and the orphan. Threshing floors are also places where God appears or is sought (Judges 6:37; 2 Samuel 24:16–25). Two kings on thrones, in royal robes, with four hundred prophets performing before them, is a scene of state theater.

a: horns of iron
p: Zedekiah acts out his prophecy with iron horns: Israel as a bull goring its enemy.
b: Prophets often acted out their messages, like Jeremiah's yoke (Jeremiah 27:2; Jeremiah 28:10–14) or Ezekiel's model of a siege (Ezekiel 4:1–3). Horns stand for strength, and Moses' blessing on the northern tribes of Joseph says "With them he will butt the peoples" (Deuteronomy 33:17). Zedekiah applies an old blessing of the north to Ahab's war. The danger of such prophets is that they quote the tradition correctly and apply it falsely.

a: the prophets speak with one mouth
p: The messenger urges Micaiah to agree with the rest. Truth is not decided by majority.
b: The king's messenger means well: one voice against four hundred is dangerous, and the king hates Micaiah already. But the phrase "with one mouth" also reveals the problem: the prophets speak like a chorus. Micaiah's reply (22:14) states the rule of true prophecy given in Deuteronomy, that the prophet speaks only what God commands (Deuteronomy 18:18). In the New Testament Peter and John say the same to the council: we cannot stop speaking what we have seen and heard (Acts 4:19–20).

a: "Go up and win," he told him.
p: Micaiah first repeats the court prophets' words. The king hears at once that he does not mean it.
b: Micaiah says word for word what the four hundred said (22:12). Yet the king answers, "How often do I have to put you under oath to speak only the truth?" (22:16). Most readers think Micaiah spoke with obvious sarcasm, and the king knew it. Others suggest that Micaiah first gave the answer the king wanted, to show how empty it was, or that God allowed him to speak the lie before revealing the truth, which fits the vision he goes on to tell (22:22).

a: like a flock with no shepherd
p: The shepherd is the king. Micaiah's vision of scattered sheep announces the king's death.
b: Moses asked God for a leader "so that the LORD's community will not be like sheep with no one to shepherd them" (Numbers 27:17). In the ancient world kings were called shepherds, and "These have no masters" means the king will fall. Ezekiel uses the image of Israel's failed kings (Ezekiel 34:5), and Zechariah speaks of the shepherd struck and the sheep scattered (Zechariah 13:7). In the gospels Jesus sees the crowds "like sheep without a shepherd" and has pity on them (Mark 6:34; Matthew 9:36), and he applies Zechariah's words to his own death (Mark 14:27).
r: Numbers 27:17; Ezekiel 34:5–6; Zechariah 13:7; Mark 6:34; Matthew 9:36; Mark 14:27

a: all the army of heaven
p: Micaiah sees the LORD enthroned among the army of heaven, deciding Ahab's fate.
b: Two kings sit on thrones at Samaria's gate (22:10); Micaiah sees a greater King on a greater throne, with "all the army of heaven" on his right and left. The scene is one of the clearest Old Testament pictures of the divine council: God presiding over heavenly beings who discuss and carry out his decisions (Job 1:6–12; Psalm 82:1; Isaiah 6:1–8). Scholars compare the assembly of the gods under El in the Ugaritic texts; others stress that here the beings have no power except what the LORD gives. Jeremiah later says the false prophets have not "taken a stand in the council of the LORD" (Jeremiah 23:18, 23:22); Micaiah claims he has.

a: Who will lure Ahab
p: The verb patah means to persuade, entice or seduce, often by fooling someone.
b: Patah covers a range from "persuade" to "deceive": it is used of seducing a woman (Exodus 22:16), of Delilah coaxing Samson's secret out of him (Judges 16:5), and of Jeremiah's cry, "You enticed me, LORD, and I was enticed" (Jeremiah 20:7, in a fresh rendering). Ezekiel says that if a prophet is "enticed," the LORD has enticed him, as a judgment on those who seek him while holding on to idols (Ezekiel 14:9). The choice of word in English ("lure," "entice," "deceive," "persuade") changes how hard the theological question sounds. This translation uses "lure" because the spirit does use a lie (22:22).

a: Then the spirit came out
p: Hebrew "the spirit" sounds like a known one. Readers have named an angel, the spirit of prophecy, Satan, even Naboth.
b: Four main answers have been given. (1) One of the heavenly beings of the council, an angel sent on a task, as in Job 1 (most modern commentators). (2) The spirit of prophecy itself, here taking the form of a false message; compare "the spirit of uncleanness" that God removes from the prophets in Zechariah 13:2. (3) Satan or a demon, as many Christian writers and some Jewish ones held, reading the scene alongside Job 1. (4) The Talmud's surprising answer: it was the spirit of Naboth the Jezreelite, seeking justice against Ahab, and God told it "Go out," that is, out of my presence, since no liar may stay before me (Bavli Sanhedrin 89a; Bavli Shabbat 149b; compare Psalm 101:7).

a: a lying spirit
p: Scripture says God does not lie. How can he send a lying spirit? Five answers, each held by serious readers.
b: "God is not a man, that he should lie" (Numbers 23:19; see Titus 1:2). Five answers: (1) God permits a deceiving being to work as judgment on a king who has rejected the truth; Paul speaks of God sending "a power of delusion" on those who refused to love the truth (2 Thessalonians 2:11), and Calvin cites this scene for God's rule over evil spirits. (2) The vision itself is the truth: by telling Ahab about the lying spirit, God warns him plainly, and Ahab goes anyway (R. W. L. Moberly). (3) The scene is a prophetic parable explaining why the court prophets were wrong, not a literal debate in heaven. (4) Early Israel traced harm as well as good to the one God (Isaiah 45:7; 2 Samuel 24:1); later texts give such work to Satan (1 Chronicles 21:1). (5) J. J. M. Roberts shows that the ancient Near East accepted divine deception as part of judgment.
r: Numbers 23:19; 2 Thessalonians 2:9–12; Ezekiel 14:9; Isaiah 45:7; 1 Chronicles 21:1; Titus 1:2

a: The LORD has spoken disaster against you.
p: Micaiah ends by telling Ahab plainly what will happen. The king still has a choice.
b: However one explains the lying spirit, the end of Micaiah's speech is not a lie. He says outright that the court prophets are deceived and that the LORD has spoken disaster. Many readers see in this the mercy of the story: Ahab is told the truth in full, as he was told by Elijah (21:21) and by the prophet of 20:42. Like Pharaoh, whose heart is both hardened by God and hardened by himself (Exodus 8:15; Exodus 9:12), Ahab chooses to believe the four hundred.

a: struck Micaiah on the cheek
t: A prophet struck on the cheek
p: Zedekiah slaps Micaiah in front of the kings. Readers have compared the slap given to Jesus at his trial.
b: A blow on the cheek was an insult more than an injury (Job 16:10; Lamentations 3:30). Zedekiah's question, "Which way did the LORD's Spirit cross over from me to you?", assumes that both cannot be true and that the Spirit cannot be in two places at once. Micah speaks of the ruler of Israel being struck "on the cheek with a rod" (Micah 5:1). In the gospels Jesus is struck before the high priest (John 18:22–23; Mark 14:65), and Paul before the council (Acts 23:2).
r: Job 16:10; Lamentations 3:30; Micah 5:1; John 18:22–23; Mark 14:65; Acts 23:2

a: the bread of hardship and the water of hardship
p: Literally "bread of oppression and water of oppression": the bare minimum, a punishment diet.
b: Lachats means pressure or oppression. Isaiah uses the same pair of words for the hard times the Lord sends his people (Isaiah 30:20). Ahab means a starvation ration in a cell until he comes home "in peace." The phrase "in peace" sets up Micaiah's reply: if you come back in peace at all, I am a false prophet.
orig: לֶחֶם לַחַץ וּמַיִם לַחַץ (lechem lachats umayim lachats)

a: If you really do come back in peace, the LORD has not spoken through me.
p: Micaiah stakes everything on Deuteronomy's test: a word that does not come true was not from the LORD.
b: Deuteronomy says: "When the prophet speaks in the name of the LORD and the thing does not happen or come true, that is a word the LORD has not spoken" (Deuteronomy 18:22). Micaiah appeals to exactly this. The test can only be applied afterward, which is why the story ends in 22:35–38 with the details of Ahab's death "just as the LORD had spoken." Jeremiah makes the same appeal against Hananiah (Jeremiah 28:8–9).

a: I will disguise myself
p: Ahab tries to dodge the prophecy by disguise. Two other kings in disguise also went to their deaths.
b: Ahab half believes Micaiah: he will not stay home, but he will not be seen either. The disguise puts Jehoshaphat, in royal robes, in danger in his place. Saul also disguised himself before his last battle ("Saul made himself unrecognizable by putting on different clothes", 1 Samuel 28:8), and Josiah disguised himself at Megiddo, where archers shot him (2 Chronicles 35:22–23). The rabbis and the church fathers alike read the story as a lesson that no disguise hides a man from God's word.

a: Jehoshaphat cried out
p: Kings does not say what Jehoshaphat cried. Chronicles says the LORD helped him and drew the attackers away.
b: His cry may have been a war cry, a shout to his men, or a prayer, and the chariot commanders realize their mistake (22:33). The Chronicler, who often stresses that God answers those who cry to him, reads it as a prayer: "Jehoshaphat cried out. The LORD came to his aid; God coaxed them away from him" (2 Chronicles 18:31). The verb behind "coaxed them away" is the one used of Jezebel stirring Ahab up (21:25), and Chronicles has already used it of Ahab coaxing Jehoshaphat into this war (2 Chronicles 18:2). See the variant on this verse.

a: with no special aim
p: Letummo means "in his simplicity": the archer shot without aiming at the king. Chance did what God had said.
b: The archer drew his bow letummo, literally "in his innocence" (compare 2 Samuel 15:11, men who went with Absalom "in their innocence," knowing nothing). He did not know whom he hit. The arrow found the one gap in the king's armor, between the joints and the breastplate. The narrator does not say God guided the arrow; he only says that a disguised king, hidden from thirty-two chariot captains, was found by a random shot. Proverbs puts it: the lot is cast into the lap, but the decision is the LORD's (Proverbs 16:33).

a: between the joints of his armor and the breastplate
p: Kings wore coats of bronze scales. An arrow could pass between the scales or at the joints.
b: The shiryon was a coat of small bronze or iron scales sewn onto leather or cloth, like Goliath's (1 Samuel 17:5). Such armor is known from Egypt, Mesopotamia and Nuzi, and its scales have been found in excavations. The weak points were where pieces joined: at the arms, the neck and the waist. The Hebrew devaqim, "joinings," may mean the attachments between the coat and a lower skirt of armor.

a: The king was kept standing up in the chariot
p: Ahab stays upright in his chariot all day while he bleeds to death. Is it courage, or a cover-up?
b: If the king had been carried off, his army might have broken. Ahab, or his driver, keeps him standing in view of Aram until evening. Some readers find in this Ahab's most noble moment, a brave death for his troops; others see a last attempt to hide the truth, which fails at sunset (22:36). Chronicles says he stood "facing Aram until evening" and died at sunset (2 Chronicles 18:34). The blood pooling in the chariot prepares for the dogs of 22:38.

a: The dogs licked up his blood
p: The narrator sees the dogs at the pool of Samaria as the fulfillment of Elijah's word in 21:19.
b: The phrase "according to the word the LORD had spoken" points back to Elijah (21:19) and perhaps to Micaiah (22:17). Ahab's blood is licked by dogs, but at Samaria, not at Jezreel, and the prophecy said "right where" Naboth's blood was licked; see the note on 21:19. The bathing prostitutes add disgrace: the king's blood mixed with the water where they washed. Other readings of the line are given in the variant on this verse, including the KJV's "they washed his armour."

a: the ivory house he built
p: Excavations at Samaria found hundreds of carved ivory pieces that once decorated royal furniture and walls.
b: Excavators at Samaria in the 1930s (the joint expedition led by John W. Crowfoot) found more than five hundred fragments of carved ivory in the palace area: plaques with lotus flowers, sphinxes, winged figures and the Egyptian child-god Horus, in Phoenician style. Most date to the ninth or eighth century BC. A "house of ivory" means a palace with ivory inlays, not one built of ivory. Amos condemns "the houses of ivory" and those who lie on "beds of ivory" in Samaria (Amos 3:15; Amos 6:4).

a: Ahab lay down with his fathers
t: A peaceful death formula for a violent death
p: "Lay down with his fathers" is the formula Kings uses for most kings. Its use here has puzzled scholars.
b: Kings normally says that a king "lay down with his fathers" when he died, and some scholars think the phrase is used only of kings who died in peace, not of those killed in battle or murdered. If so, its use for Ahab is strange after 22:35–37, and J. Maxwell Miller and others take it as a sign that the battle story was first told of another king and later attached to Ahab. Other scholars answer that the formula simply means "died and was buried": Amaziah, who was murdered, is also said to have lain down with his fathers (2 Kings 14:19–22). The question remains open.

a: In the fourth year of Ahab king of Israel
p: Kings dates each reign by the reign of the king next door. The numbers are hard to fit together exactly.
b: The writer of Kings cross-dates the two kingdoms: Jehoshaphat begins in Ahab's fourth year, Ahaziah in Jehoshaphat's seventeenth (22:51). The totals do not add up neatly, and scholars explain the gaps by co-regencies (a son ruling with his father), different ways of counting the first year, and different calendars. Edwin Thiele's widely used system dates Ahab about 874–853 BC and Jehoshaphat about 872–848 BC, with a co-regency with Asa. The Greek gives a different date for Jehoshaphat; see the variant.

a: the high places were not removed
p: Even good kings of Judah left the local shrines standing. Only Hezekiah and Josiah removed them.
b: The "high places" (bamot) were local shrines, often on hills, where the LORD (and sometimes other gods) was worshiped with sacrifice. Deuteronomy demands worship at one chosen place (Deuteronomy 12:2–14), and Kings judges each king of Judah by it. Jehoshaphat, like Asa, gets a good verdict with this one reservation (15:14). Chronicles says Jehoshaphat did remove the high places (2 Chronicles 17:6) but also that they remained (2 Chronicles 20:33), perhaps meaning shrines to other gods were removed and shrines to the LORD were not.

a: the shrine men
p: The qedeshim, "holy ones," are often called "male shrine prostitutes." Whether sacred prostitution existed is debated.
b: Qadesh means "consecrated one." These men were attached to shrines (14:24; 15:12; 2 Kings 23:7), and Deuteronomy forbids Israelites to be one (Deuteronomy 23:17). Older scholars, reading Herodotus and others, believed temple prostitution was common in the ancient Near East, and many translations say "male cult prostitutes." Recent studies, such as Stephanie Budin's, argue that clear evidence for sacred prostitution is lacking, and that the qedeshim may have been cult servants of some other kind. This translation uses the neutral "shrine men."

a: Tarshish ships
p: A "Tarshish ship" was a large sea-going vessel, named for a far-off port in the west.
b: Tarshish was a distant port, often placed at Tartessos in southern Spain, or in Sardinia; Jonah sails for it (Jonah 1:3). A "Tarshish ship" came to mean any large merchant ship, even one sailing south from Ezion-geber on the Red Sea to Ophir, as Solomon's did (10:22; 9:26–28). Jehoshaphat tries to revive Solomon's gold trade, and the ships are wrecked in port. Chronicles says that Jehoshaphat built the fleet with Ahaziah and that a prophet, Eliezer, foretold its wreck because of the alliance (2 Chronicles 20:35–37); Kings says Jehoshaphat refused Ahaziah's offer (22:49).

a: Ahaziah son of Ahab became king over Israel
p: The book stops in the middle of Ahaziah's reign. In Hebrew, Kings was one book; the split came much later.
b: The story of Ahaziah goes straight on in 2 Kings 1, where he falls through a lattice and sends to ask Baal-zebub, and Elijah meets his messengers. Kings was one book in the Hebrew tradition. The Greek translators divided Samuel and Kings into four "Books of Kingdoms," probably because of scroll length, and this division passed into Latin Bibles. Hebrew Bibles adopted the split into 1 and 2 Kings only in the printed editions of the early 1500s. The break here is a convenience, not an ending.

a: He served Baal and bowed down to him
p: Ahaziah walks in the ways of both his father and his mother. The Baal story continues in 2 Kings.
b: The verdict on Ahaziah names "his mother's road" as well as his father's (22:52); Jezebel is still alive. Baal worship goes on until Jehu (2 Kings 10:18–28), and Ahaziah's first act in 2 Kings is to send to Baal-zebub of Ekron for an oracle (2 Kings 1:2). The book ends as it began its Elijah stories: with the question of 18:21 still unanswered by the house of Ahab.
